svg.title: Which aircraft make the strongest wake
svg.desc: Two rear-view sketches. Greatest vortex strength: heavy, slow and clean, with large vortices. Weaker wake: lighter, faster, or dirty (flaps or other devices extended), which hastens wake decay. Strength is directly proportional to weight and inversely proportional to wingspan and speed, with maximum strength during takeoff, climb and landing. En route events have occurred in excess of 30NM and 2000 feet lower than the generating aircraft. Avoid a hovering helicopter by at least three rotor disc diameters.
svg.text: Which aircraft make the strongest wake
The basic factors are weight and speed. Strength increases proportionately with operating weight, or
with a decrease in speed.
Greatest strength
Heavy, slow, and clean
Weaker wake
flaps out
Lighter, faster, or "dirty" (flaps or other devices
extended)
What the text says
The greatest vortex strength occurs when the
generating aircraft is heavy, slow, and clean
The turbulence from a "dirty" aircraft
configuration hastens wake decay
Strength is directly proportional to weight and
inversely proportional to wingspan and speed
Maximum strength occurs during the takeoff, climb,
and landing phases, when the AOA is at the highest
Flaps, other wing configuration devices, and speed
all change an aircraft's vortex characteristics
Why it matters to you
Vortices from larger aircraft can impose rolling
moments exceeding the roll-control authority of the
encountering aircraft
Turbulence within the vortices can damage aircraft
components and equipment if encountered at close
range
Pilots must envision the location of the vortex
wake and adjust the flight path accordingly
En route
More "Super" (A380) and "Heavy" (B-747, B-777,
A340, etc.) aircraft operate in the NAS
Wake events have occurred in excess of 30NM and
2000 feet lower than the generating aircraft
Reduced air density at altitude may give wake
strength comparable to the terminal area
At cruise speed there is less time for the wake to
decay before a trailing aircraft meets it
Not only airplanes
Avoid a hovering helicopter by at least three rotor
disc diameters (its down wash is similar to an
airplane's vortices)
In forward flight a helicopter makes a pair of
strong, high-speed trailing vortices; its slow
forward airspeeds can generate exceptionally strong
wake turbulence
